title: The while Loop
description: Repeat for as long as a condition holds, when you cannot count the turns in advance.

content.value: When You Do Not Know How Many Times
A `while` loop holds just one thing in its brackets: a condition. It repeats the body for as long as that condition is true.

items.sub: Ten rows, five questions, `n` numbers, a countdown.
Until the user types 0, until the input is valid, until the digits run out.

items.title: for
items.text: All three parts in the brackets.

items.title: while

content.title: The same loop, written two ways
content.caption: The three parts did not disappear, they moved. The start goes above the loop, the condition stays in the brackets, and the update becomes a line in the body.

steps.note: The start value is set above the loop.
Check `1 <= 3`: true, so run the body.
The update is an ordinary line now.

content.title: Watch the while loop

content.value: A `for` loop cannot forget its `i++`. A `while` loop can. Then the condition never changes and the loop never ends.

items.title: Never ends
Ends

content.title: Ends vs never ends
content.caption: For every `while` you write, point at the line that will one day make the condition false. If you cannot, the loop does not end.

content.value: A loop that never ends is an **infinite loop**. It floods the output with the same line until the run is cut off after a few seconds. If that happens, look for a `while` whose body never changes its condition.
content.title: Infinite loops

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `n` goes 10, 6, 2, then -2. Only then is `n > 0` false, so the loop stops and prints -2.

content.value: The user types numbers to add up, and types 0 to finish. A value that means "stop" like this is called a **sentinel**.

content.title: The shape of a sentinel loop
content.caption: Miss the read at the bottom and you get an infinite loop. Miss the read at the top and `n` holds a leftover garbage value, so the first test is nonsense.
Sample run: type 4, 6, then 0. It prints `You entered 2 numbers.` and `Total: 10`. Type 0 first and the body never runs: 0 numbers, total 0.

content.value: The same shape refuses bad input: `while (age < 1 || age > 120)` asks again. The condition is true when the input is **wrong**. Declare `age` above the loop so it still exists afterwards.
content.title: Keep asking until it is valid

content.value: `n % 10` gives the last digit. `n / 10` chops it off, because whole-number division drops the remainder. A `while` loop repeats that until no digits are left.

content.title: Chop off one digit per turn
content.outro: Each turn shortens the number, so the loop always moves towards stopping. Add `digits++` in the body and it counts the digits too.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: Each turn pushes the last digit onto `reversed`: 3, then 32, then 321. Then `n` is 0 and the loop stops.

content.value: Work on a copy like `left` if you still need the original number later. And watch for 0: `0 > 0` is false, so the body never runs and a digit counter says 0 digits. A `do while`, next lesson, can fix that.

quiz.question: When is a `while` loop the better choice than a `for` loop?
options: When the loop ends on an event rather than after a known number of turns
When the block has more than one line in it
quiz.explain: A count belongs in a `for`. Waiting for a sentinel value, valid input or a game to finish belongs in a `while`.

quiz.question: What makes a `while` loop infinite?
options: The loop has no counter variable
Nothing inside the block ever makes the condition false
quiz.explain: The condition is only re-tested, never changed by itself. Something in the block has to move it towards false.

quiz.question: In a sentinel loop, why do you read the input once before the loop as well as inside it?
options: So the condition has a real value to test on the very first check
To make the loop run at least once
quiz.explain: The first read gives the condition something real to look at, and the read at the bottom of the block refreshes it for the next test.

quiz.question: What does `n % 10` give you, and what does `n / 10` do, for an int n?
options: The first digit, and the number divided as a decimal
The last digit, and the number with that digit removed
The number of digits, and the digit sum
quiz.explain: The remainder after dividing by ten is the last digit, and whole-number division throws that digit away. Together they walk through a number digit by digit.

quiz.question: Why is a validation variable like `age` declared above the loop rather than inside it?
options: Because cin can only be read outside a loop
So the condition can be changed later
So the value the loop accepted still exists after the loop ends
quiz.explain: A variable declared inside the block dies at the closing brace, so the rest of the program would have nothing to use.
